recipes.title: Chicken Tikka Masala
recipes.blurb: Charred spiced chicken in a warm, creamy tomato gravy with real backbone from toasted whole spices. Marinate it in the morning and dinner practically makes itself.

items: 2 lb (900 g) boneless skinless chicken thighs, cut into 2 in (5 cm) pieces
3 tbsp (45 ml) ghee or neutral oil
1 large yellow onion (10 oz / 285 g), finely diced
4 cups (660 g) cooked basmati rice, for serving

instructions.title: Build the marinade
instructions.text: Whisk the 1 cup yogurt, 2 tbsp lemon juice, 2 tbsp ginger, 6 minced garlic cloves, 2 tsp cumin, 2 tsp paprika, 1 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp cayenne and 2 tsp salt in a large bowl until it is a uniform rust-orange paste. Use whole-milk yogurt, because low-fat versions are thin and watery and will slide off the chicken instead of clinging. It should be thick enough to coat a spoon heavily.

instructions.title: Marinate for hours
instructions.text: Add the chicken pieces and turn them until each one is thickly coated, then cover and refrigerate for at least 4 hours and ideally overnight. Yogurt tenderizes gently and slowly, so long marinating actually improves the texture rather than turning the surface to mush. Cutting the thighs into large 2 in (5 cm) pieces means they can char hard on the outside while staying juicy inside.

instructions.title: Start the onions
instructions.text: Heat the 3 tbsp ghee in a heavy 5 qt (4.7 L) pot over medium heat and add the diced onion with a pinch of salt. Cook for 10 to 12 minutes, stirring every couple of minutes, until deeply softened and golden brown at the edges. This is longer than you think it needs and it is the flavor foundation of the entire dish, so do not cut it short at five minutes.

instructions.title: Bloom the ground spices
instructions.text: Add the 2 tbsp ginger and 6 minced garlic cloves and cook 90 seconds, then add the 2 tsp coriander, 2 tsp cumin, 1 tbsp paprika and 2 tsp garam masala and stir constantly for 45 seconds. The pot will smell suddenly enormous and the spices will darken a shade. Ground spices burn in well under a minute at this heat, so have the tomatoes open and ready to go in.

instructions.title: Add tomatoes and simmer
instructions.text: Pour in the can of crushed tomatoes and the 1 1/2 tsp salt, scraping the bottom to lift every bit of stuck spice. Bring it to a simmer, then lower the heat and cook uncovered for 20 minutes, stirring occasionally. The sauce should darken from bright red to brick and thicken enough that a spoon dragged through leaves a trail for a second.

instructions.title: Preheat the broiler
instructions.text: Position an oven rack 6 in (15 cm) below the broiler element and heat the broiler to high for 5 minutes. Line a sheet pan with foil and fit a wire rack inside it. The rack matters: it lets the marinade drip away so the chicken blisters and chars rather than sitting in a puddle and steaming.

instructions.title: Broil the chicken hard
instructions.text: Shake the excess marinade off each piece and lay them out with at least 1/2 in (1 cm) of space between them. Broil for 8 to 10 minutes without opening the door, until the tops are blackened in spots. Those charred edges are the tikka part of tikka masala and they carry a smokiness the sauce cannot produce on its own, so be brave and let them go dark.

instructions.title: Flip and check
instructions.text: Turn each piece with tongs and broil for another 5 to 7 minutes. Check the largest piece with an instant-read thermometer; it must reach 165°F (74°C). Set the pan aside and do not discard the juices that collect in the foil, because they are pure concentrated flavor.

instructions.title: Blend or leave rustic
instructions.text: For a restaurant-smooth gravy, blend the tomato sauce with an immersion blender until silky, about 30 seconds. For a homestyle texture, leave it chunky with visible onion. Either is legitimate; blended sauces coat the chicken more evenly while rustic ones have more bite. If you use a countertop blender, vent the lid and work in batches, because hot liquid expands and can blow the top off.

instructions.title: Add the cream
instructions.text: Lower the heat and stir in the 1 cup heavy cream and 1 tbsp butter, whisking until the sauce turns a soft coral orange. Keep it below a simmer from here on, around 180°F (82°C), because boiling will curdle the cream into grainy flecks. Taste it now, before the chicken goes in, and correct the salt.

instructions.title: Combine and simmer gently
instructions.text: Add the broiled chicken along with every drop of juice from the sheet pan and simmer very gently for 8 to 10 minutes, uncovered. The chicken releases some of its marinade flavor into the gravy while it soaks the sauce up in return, and this exchange is what makes the finished dish taste unified rather than like two separate things. Stir a couple of times so nothing catches on the bottom.

instructions.title: Finish and rest
instructions.text: Stir in the 1 tsp lemon juice and half the cilantro, then take the pot off the heat and let it sit 10 minutes. That rest lets the sauce thicken and the flavors settle, and tikka masala genuinely improves in those ten minutes. Scatter the remaining cilantro over the top and serve over hot basmati rice with naan alongside.

tips: Marinate overnight if you possibly can. Four hours works, but twelve gives noticeably more tender, more deeply seasoned chicken.
No broiler? Grill the chicken over high heat for 4 minutes per side, or sear it in a smoking hot cast iron skillet. The char is not optional flavor.
Make-ahead: the sauce keeps 4 days refrigerated and freezes for 3 months without the cream. Add the cream when you reheat so it never gets boiled twice.
Cayenne is the heat dial. One teaspoon is medium-warm; use 1/2 tsp for mild or 2 tsp if you want it to bite back.
Skewer the marinated chicken and cook it over charcoal if you have a grill going. That is closest to a real tandoor and the difference is obvious.
recipes.keyTemp: Chicken must reach 165°F (74°C) at the center of the largest piece, with blackened blistered edges from the broiler. Hold the finished sauce below a simmer, around 180°F (82°C), so the cream stays smooth instead of curdling.
recipes.pairing: Basmati rice, garlic naan, and a cold IPA or a chilled off-dry Riesling.

recipes.title: Beef Pho with Rice Noodles
recipes.blurb: A clear, deeply spiced beef broth built over an afternoon, poured boiling over rice noodles and raw slices of steak. This is the weekend project that fills the whole apartment with star anise.

items: 4 lb (1.8 kg) beef marrow and knuckle bones
1 lb (450 g) beef oxtail or short rib
2 lb (900 g) beef brisket, in one piece
2 large yellow onions (1 lb / 450 g total), halved
1 piece fresh ginger (4 in / 10 cm), halved lengthwise
3 black cardamom pods, or 4 green cardamom pods
3 tbsp (45 ml) fish sauce, plus more to taste
1 oz (30 g) yellow rock sugar, about a 1 in (2.5 cm) piece
2 tsp (12 g) kosher salt, plus more to taste
1 lb (450 g) dried flat rice noodles (banh pho), 1/4 in (5 mm) wide
12 oz (340 g) beef eye of round, frozen 30 minutes and sliced paper thin

instructions.title: Parboil the bones
instructions.text: Put the bones and oxtail in a large stockpot, cover with cold water, and bring to a hard boil over high heat for 10 minutes. Gray foam and scum will rise to the top in alarming quantity. This step exists purely to purge blood and impurities, and it is the difference between a crystal clear pho broth and a cloudy murky one.

instructions.title: Scrub the bones clean
instructions.text: Dump the whole pot into the sink through a colander and rinse each bone under running water, scrubbing off any dark bits clinging to the surface. Scrub the pot itself clean too, because the residue sticks to the sides. Do not skip the scrubbing; leftover scum will cloud the broth all over again.

instructions.title: Char the onions and ginger
instructions.text: Set the onion halves and ginger cut side down directly on a gas burner over high flame, or under a broiler 4 in (10 cm) from the element, and cook 8 to 12 minutes until blackened in patches and soft. Turn them so several sides char. This charring is not optional decoration; it caramelizes sugars and adds the smoky sweetness that makes pho taste like pho. Rinse off any loose ash and set aside.

instructions.title: Toast the spices
instructions.text: Toast the 6 star anise, cinnamon stick, 6 cloves, 1 tbsp coriander seeds, 1 tsp fennel seeds and 3 black cardamom pods in a dry skillet over medium heat for 3 to 4 minutes, shaking often, until intensely fragrant. Watch closely because they go from toasty to burnt fast, and burnt star anise will make six quarts of broth taste like ash. Tie them into a spice bag or a square of cheesecloth so you can fish them out later.

instructions.title: Start the long simmer
instructions.text: Return the scrubbed bones to the clean pot, add the 6 qt cold water, and bring it up to a bare simmer over medium heat, which takes about 30 minutes. Add the charred onion and ginger and the spice bag. Starting from cold water lets the proteins release slowly and rise as a raft you can skim, rather than clouding the broth all at once.

instructions.title: Hold a bare simmer and skim
instructions.text: Adjust the heat until you see only occasional lazy bubbles breaking the surface, roughly 195 to 205°F (90 to 96°C), and never let it reach a rolling boil. Skim the surface every 20 minutes for the first hour, then every 45 minutes after. A boiling pot emulsifies fat into the liquid and turns it permanently cloudy and greasy, and no amount of straining later will fix it.

instructions.title: Add and remove the brisket
instructions.text: Slide the brisket into the pot after the first hour of simmering and cook it for 90 minutes to 2 hours, until a fork slides in with little resistance. Pull it out, plunge it into a bowl of ice water for 10 minutes to stop the cooking and keep it from graying, then wrap and refrigerate. Cooling it firm makes it far easier to slice thin later.

instructions.title: Simmer, then season
instructions.text: Let the broth continue at that bare simmer for a total of 5 to 6 hours, topping up with hot water if the level drops below the bones. In the last hour, add the 3 tbsp fish sauce, the 1 oz rock sugar and 2 tsp salt. Seasoning late means you are salting a broth that has already reduced, so you do not overshoot and end up with something inedible.

instructions.title: Strain and defat
instructions.text: Pull out the bones and spice bag, then strain the broth through a fine mesh sieve lined with cheesecloth into a clean pot. Let it settle 10 minutes and skim the fat off the top with a wide spoon, or chill it and lift the solid cap off. Taste it now: it should be aromatic, savory and slightly sweet, and you should want to drink it plain from a mug.

instructions.title: Slice the raw beef paper thin
instructions.text: Freeze the eye of round for 30 minutes until firm, then slice it across the grain as thinly as you possibly can, ideally under 1/8 in (3 mm) so it is nearly translucent. Lay the slices flat on a plate and refrigerate until the moment you serve. Thin enough and the boiling broth cooks them through in seconds right in the bowl.

instructions.title: Cook the noodles to order
instructions.text: Bring a separate large pot of water to a boil and cook the rice noodles for 6 to 8 minutes according to the package, then drain. Cook them just before serving and portion them straight into bowls, because noodles that sit around clump into a solid mass. Never cook noodles in your broth; the starch they release will cloud six hours of careful work in about two minutes.

instructions.title: Slice the brisket
instructions.text: Take the chilled brisket out and slice it across the grain about 1/8 in (3 mm) thick. Cold meat slices cleanly where warm meat shreds and tears. Arrange the slices with the raw eye of round on a platter along with everything else you need for assembly.

instructions.title: Assemble the bowls
instructions.text: Bring the strained broth back to a hard rolling boil, which is the one time boiling is correct. Divide the hot noodles among six large bowls, top each with sliced brisket and a layer of raw eye of round, then ladle 2 cups of furiously boiling broth over the top. The raw slices should go from red to gray-brown within about 20 seconds. If you would rather not serve barely-cooked beef, blanch the slices in the boiling broth for 30 seconds first so they reach 145°F (63°C).

instructions.title: Garnish at the table
instructions.text: Put the bean sprouts, Thai basil, lime wedges, sliced scallions, jalapenos and cilantro on a platter in the middle of the table so everyone builds their own bowl. Add herbs a few at a time as you eat rather than all at once, so they stay fresh and fragrant instead of wilting into the broth. Hoisin and sriracha belong in a small side dish for dipping the meat, not squeezed into the broth, though nobody will stop you.

tips: The parboil-and-scrub step is what separates homemade pho from restaurant pho. It takes fifteen minutes and it is the single highest-value thing you can do for clarity.
Make-ahead: the broth is the whole project and it keeps 5 days refrigerated or 3 months frozen. Freeze it in quart containers and a bowl of pho is twenty minutes away any weeknight.
Yellow rock sugar has a cleaner, less cloying sweetness than granulated. If you cannot find it, use 1 tbsp of granulated sugar instead.
Ask the butcher for a mix of marrow bones and knuckle bones. Marrow gives richness and knuckles give collagen and body, and you want both.
If your broth still comes out cloudy, the culprit is almost always heat. Keep it at a lazy bare simmer where a bubble breaks every second or two, not a bubbling boil.
recipes.keyTemp: Hold the broth at 195 to 205°F (90 to 96°C) throughout the simmer, never a rolling boil. Brisket is tender around 195°F (91°C) internal, and the raw eye of round slices should be blanched to 145°F (63°C) if you want them fully cooked rather than just flashed in boiling broth.
recipes.pairing: A cup of the plain broth on the side, Vietnamese iced coffee afterward, and plenty of lime and herbs on the table.

recipes.title: Mongolian Beef with Scallions
recipes.blurb: Crisp cornstarch-coated beef in a dark, glossy soy and brown sugar glaze with a pile of scallions. Thirty minutes start to finish and it disappears faster than that.

items: 1 1/2 lb (680 g) flank steak, sliced 1/4 in (6 mm) against the grain
2/3 cup (145 g) dark brown sugar, packed
1/2 cup (120 ml) neutral oil, for shallow frying
1 tbsp (15 ml) neutral oil, for the sauce
8 scallions, cut into 2 in (5 cm) lengths
4 cups (660 g) hot cooked jasmine rice, for serving

instructions.title: Slice the flank steak
instructions.text: Chill the flank steak in the freezer for 15 minutes so it firms up, then find the grain and cut straight across it into slices about 1/4 in (6 mm) thick. Angle your knife at roughly 45 degrees to get wider slices that hold more coating. Cutting against the grain shortens the muscle fibers, and with a lean cut like flank that is the only thing standing between tender and chewy.

instructions.title: Dry the beef thoroughly
instructions.text: Blot the slices with paper towels until they no longer feel wet, then season with the 1/2 tsp salt. Cornstarch will not adhere to a damp surface; it turns into a slimy paste that slides off in the oil. Two minutes of blotting here saves the entire texture of the dish.

instructions.title: Coat in cornstarch
instructions.text: Toss the beef with the 1/2 cup cornstarch in a large bowl until every slice is chalky white with no bare spots, then shake off the excess in a colander. A thin even coat fries into a crisp shell that grabs the sauce; a thick clumpy one goes gummy. Let the coated beef rest 10 minutes so the starch hydrates slightly and clings better.

instructions.title: Mix the sauce
instructions.text: Stir the 1/2 cup soy sauce, 1/2 cup water, 2/3 cup dark brown sugar, 1 tbsp ginger, 5 minced garlic cloves and 1/4 tsp red pepper flakes together in a bowl until the sugar mostly dissolves. It will look alarmingly sweet, and that is correct, since it reduces down to a balanced glaze. Low-sodium soy sauce matters here because you are reducing a half cup of it and regular soy would end up brutally salty.

instructions.title: Set up your station
instructions.text: Put the coated beef, sauce bowl, scallions and a wire rack set over a sheet pan all within arm's reach of the stove. Start the rice now if you have not. From the moment the oil is hot this dish moves quickly and you will be using tongs with both hands.

instructions.title: Heat the frying oil
instructions.text: Pour the 1/2 cup oil into a 12 in (30 cm) skillet or wok and heat over medium-high until it shimmers and a pinch of cornstarch dropped in sizzles immediately, about 350°F (175°C). This is shallow frying, not deep frying, so the oil only needs to come about 1/4 in (6 mm) up the pan. If the oil is not hot enough the coating absorbs it and turns greasy instead of crisping.

instructions.title: Fry the beef in batches
instructions.text: Lay a third of the slices in the oil in a single layer with space between them and fry for 60 to 90 seconds per side, until the edges are golden and the coating is set. Move them to the wire rack and repeat with the remaining beef. Crowding drops the oil temperature and the slices will stick together into a single mass, so three small batches beat one big one every time.

instructions.title: Pour off the oil
instructions.text: Carefully pour the frying oil into a heatproof bowl, leaving any browned bits behind, and wipe the pan with a paper towel if there is burnt cornstarch stuck to it. Return the pan to the heat with 1 tbsp of fresh oil. Cooking the sauce in old frying oil makes it heavy and greasy.

instructions.title: Reduce the sauce
instructions.text: Pour the sauce into the hot pan and bring it to a boil over medium-high heat, then let it bubble for 3 to 4 minutes, stirring, until it reduces by about a third and turns syrupy. Drag a spatula through it: the sauce should hold a clear line on the pan bottom for a second before flowing back. Watch it closely at the end, because sugar syrups go from perfect to burnt in under thirty seconds.

instructions.title: Toss the beef in the glaze
instructions.text: Add all the fried beef back to the pan and toss for 30 to 45 seconds, just until every slice is coated in dark shiny glaze. Do not linger here; the longer the crisp coating sits in liquid, the softer it gets. The beef should look lacquered, not swimming.

instructions.title: Finish with scallions and serve
instructions.text: Add the scallions, toss twice, and kill the heat so they stay bright green with a little crunch. Scatter the 1 tsp sesame seeds over the top and serve immediately over hot jasmine rice with the pan sauce spooned around. Mongolian beef is at its best in the first five minutes, so get it to the table straight from the stove.

tips: Flank is traditional, but skirt steak, sirloin or flat iron all work well. Any lean cut sliced thin against the grain is fine.
Use low-sodium soy sauce. This sauce reduces significantly and regular soy sauce will make the finished dish nearly inedible.
The sauce is very sweet by design. If you prefer it more savory, cut the brown sugar to 1/2 cup and add 1 tbsp of rice vinegar at the end.
Make-ahead: slice and coat the beef up to 2 hours ahead and keep it on a rack in the fridge. Mix the sauce up to 3 days ahead.
Broccoli or snow peas make this a full meal. Blanch 8 oz (225 g) for 2 minutes and toss them in with the scallions.
recipes.keyTemp: Beef is safe at 145°F (63°C), and slices this thin get there within about 90 seconds per side in 350°F (175°C) oil. Go by the coating: pull the slices when the crust is golden and set, because overcooked flank turns tough no matter how it is sauced.
recipes.pairing: Steamed jasmine rice, quick-blanched broccoli, and a cold lager to cut the sweetness.

recipes.title: Beef Bibimbap with Crispy Rice
recipes.blurb: A bowl of seasoned vegetables, marinated beef and a fried egg over rice that crackles against a hot pan. You stir it all together with gochujang and it becomes something entirely new.

items: 12 oz (340 g) beef sirloin or ribeye, thinly sliced 1/8 in (3 mm)
1/2 tsp (1 g) freshly ground black pepper
1 large carrot (5 oz / 140 g), cut into matchsticks
5 oz (140 g) shiitake mushrooms, stemmed and sliced
1 medium zucchini (7 oz / 200 g), cut into matchsticks
3 tbsp (45 ml) toasted sesame oil, divided
4 cups (660 g) hot cooked short-grain white rice
2 tbsp (30 ml) toasted sesame oil, for the bowls
1 tbsp (15 ml) neutral oil, for frying the eggs
1 sheet toasted nori, cut into thin strips

instructions.title: Marinate the beef
instructions.text: Toss the sliced beef with the 2 tbsp soy sauce, 1 tbsp sesame oil, 1 tbsp brown sugar, 3 minced garlic cloves and 1/2 tsp black pepper, then refrigerate for 30 minutes while you prepare everything else. Slicing the beef at 1/8 in (3 mm) means it takes on the marinade quickly and cooks in about two minutes. If the meat is hard to slice, freeze it for 20 minutes first.

instructions.title: Understand namul
instructions.text: Each vegetable in bibimbap is cooked and seasoned separately, which is the technique called namul. Set out five small bowls, one per vegetable, and keep them separate all the way to the table. It sounds like extra work but it is the entire point: every component tastes distinctly of itself, and stirring them together at the last second is what makes the bowl interesting rather than muddy.

instructions.title: Blanch and season the spinach
instructions.text: Boil a medium pot of salted water, drop in the spinach for 30 seconds, then transfer it to ice water. Squeeze it into a tight ball and wring out every bit of water you can, then chop it and toss with 1/2 tsp sesame oil, a pinch of the salt and a third of the minced garlic. Wet spinach will leak into the rice and make the bottom soggy, so squeeze it harder than seems reasonable.

instructions.title: Blanch the bean sprouts
instructions.text: Using the same pot of boiling water, cook the mung bean sprouts for 2 minutes, then drain and rinse under cold water. Squeeze them gently and toss with 1/2 tsp sesame oil, a pinch of salt and another third of the garlic. They should stay crunchy, since raw sprouts taste grassy but overcooked ones go limp and sad.

instructions.title: Saute the carrots
instructions.text: Heat 1 tsp of the sesame oil in a skillet over medium-high, add the carrot matchsticks and a pinch of salt, and cook for 2 minutes until they turn bright orange and just start to soften. Tip them into their bowl. Cook the vegetables in order from lightest to darkest so you do not have to wash the pan between each one.

instructions.title: Saute the zucchini
instructions.text: Add another 1 tsp sesame oil, then the zucchini matchsticks and a pinch of salt, and cook 2 minutes until barely tender and still bright green. Zucchini is mostly water and will turn to mush in another minute, so pull it early. Salt it lightly, because it releases water as it sits.

instructions.title: Brown the mushrooms
instructions.text: Add 1 tbsp sesame oil, then the sliced shiitakes and a pinch of salt, and cook 4 to 5 minutes without stirring much, until they release their liquid, it cooks off, and the edges brown. Stir in the last of the garlic for the final 30 seconds. Mushrooms need a hot pan and patience; constant stirring keeps them pale and squeaky.

instructions.title: Cook the beef
instructions.text: Wipe the skillet, turn the heat to high, and spread the marinated beef in a single layer. Cook 60 seconds without touching it, then toss for 60 to 90 seconds more until browned and just cooked through. Beef is safe at 145°F (63°C) and slices this thin race past it, so pull them the moment the edges caramelize.

instructions.title: Mix the gochujang sauce
instructions.text: Whisk the 3 tbsp gochujang, 1 tbsp sesame oil, 1 tbsp water, 1 tbsp sugar, 1 tbsp rice vinegar and the grated garlic clove until smooth and pourable. Taste it: it should be spicy, sweet and tangy in about equal measure. This sauce is what unifies the whole bowl, so make more than you think you need and put extra on the table.

instructions.title: Crisp the rice
instructions.text: Heat 1/2 tbsp of sesame oil in a small nonstick or cast iron skillet over medium heat, add 1 cup of the hot rice, and press it into an even layer. Cook undisturbed for 4 to 5 minutes until you hear a steady crackling and the bottom is golden and crisp. Slide it into a warmed bowl crust side down and repeat for each serving. If you own a stone dolsot, oil it and heat it to about 400°F (205°C) instead, then press the rice in.

instructions.title: Fry the eggs sunny side up
instructions.text: Heat the 1 tbsp neutral oil in a nonstick skillet over medium heat and crack in the eggs. Cook 2 to 3 minutes until the whites are fully set and opaque but the yolks are still liquid, spooning a little hot oil over the whites to help them along. The runny yolk becomes part of the sauce when you stir the bowl, which is exactly the point.

instructions.title: Arrange the bowls
instructions.text: Over each bowl of crisped rice, arrange the seasoned vegetables and beef in separate wedges around the edge like spokes on a wheel, keeping the colors next to each other for contrast. Set a fried egg in the center. Take a moment with this, because the arrangement is genuinely part of the dish and it only stays pretty for about a minute.

instructions.title: Garnish and serve hot
instructions.text: Scatter the 2 tbsp sesame seeds and the nori strips over the top and bring the bowls to the table with the gochujang sauce alongside. Serve immediately while the bottom rice is still crackling. Bibimbap loses its magic if it sits, so this is a dish you plate and carry straight out.

instructions.title: Stir it all together
instructions.text: At the table, everyone adds a heaping spoonful of gochujang sauce and stirs the whole bowl vigorously with a spoon until the yolk, sauce, rice and vegetables are completely combined. Bibimbap literally means mixed rice, and the mixing is not optional. Scrape the crispy rice up from the bottom as you go so those toasted bits get distributed through every bite.

tips: Cook every vegetable separately even though it feels excessive. Together they steam into a single flavor, and the whole appeal of bibimbap is that each bite is slightly different.
Make-ahead: all the namul vegetables can be made up to 3 days in advance and kept in separate containers. Then a bowl of bibimbap is a 15 minute dinner.
For a runny yolk with less risk, use pasteurized eggs, or cook the eggs to 160°F (71°C) with a set yolk if anyone eating is pregnant, elderly or immunocompromised.
A stone dolsot bowl gives you the best crust, but a small cast iron skillet or a nonstick pan gets you eighty percent of the way there.
Leftover bulgogi, roast chicken or a can of drained tuna all work in place of the marinated beef. Bibimbap started as a way to use up side dishes.
recipes.keyTemp: Beef slices are safe at 145°F (63°C) and reach it in about 2 minutes over high heat; pull them the moment the edges caramelize. Fried eggs with fully set whites and runny yolks sit around 145°F (63°C), so use pasteurized eggs or cook them through to 160°F (71°C) if anyone at the table should avoid soft yolks.
recipes.pairing: A small bowl of kimchi, a cold Korean lager or barley tea, and extra gochujang sauce on the table.
